insights: Data quality: 96,228 rows (~3.2%) are exact duplicates of (store, date, product family) rows that differ only in event tagging — e.g. 2014-06-25 has 7,128 duplicate rows because multiple event types (World Cup + national/local tags) were written as separate records. This inflates raw sales by ~2.1%. After deduping, the panel is perfectly balanced: 54 stores × 33 families × 1,684 days = 3,000,888 records with zero missing combinations.

Network growth: Total sales grew 2.06× from $140M (2013) to $289M (2016), and average daily sales rose from $386K (2013) to $856K (2017 through Aug 15). Growth was broad-based, not just new openings — the ~46 stores operating before 2015 grew 1.28× between 2014 and 2016 on their own, while only 8 stores were added mid-panel (most in 2015).

Store concentration: Quito's 18 stores alone generated 52% of all network sales, averaging $30.9M per store vs $15.4M in Guayaquil and $4.1M in the smallest city (Puyo). The top 10 stores account for 40% of total sales while the bottom 10 contribute just 6.8%; the largest store (5.8% share) outsells the smallest by ~23×. Between-store variation explains ~53% of total sales variation — store identity matters as much as time.

Category concentration: Just 5 of 33 product families drive 79% of all revenue — Grocery I (32%), Beverages (20%), Produce (11%), Cleaning (9%), and Dairy (6%). Conversely, 7 families (BOOKS, BABY CARE, HOME APPLIANCES, HARDWARE, MAGAZINES, SCHOOL & OFFICE SUPPLIES, LADIESWEAR) together contribute less than 1% of sales, so assortment decisions should be made at family level, not network level.

Sparse/placeholder families: BOOKS shows zero sales on 97% of store-days and accumulated only $6.4K total across 54 stores over 4.7 years (vs $343M for Grocery I); BABY CARE is 94% zero with $10K total; both only started recording sales in 2016-17 ($0 in 2013-15). These appear to be inactive placeholder categories rather than real product lines — they should be excluded from assortment and demand planning.

Weekend seasonality: Saturdays run 35% and Sundays 44% above the Mon-Fri average, and Sunday alone carries 18.4% of weekly revenue (vs a flat 14.3% share). The pattern holds across cities (Quito 19.5% of sales on Sundays, Riobamba just 12.8%). Conversely, New Year's Day is the single lowest sales day four years running (sinking to $12K total on 2017-01-01 vs a ~$850K typical day) — stores appear effectively closed.

Oil price correlation is a shared-trend artifact, not a driver: daily sales correlate -0.71 with crude oil because oil fell from ~$98 to ~$43 (2015-16) as sales grew 2×. Once both series are detrended, the correlation collapses to about -0.10 (daily) / -0.19 (monthly). Also the oil series is missing all 521 Saturdays/Sundays (31% of days), so it is a weekday-only market price field — treat any oil-based sales model with caution.

April 2016 earthquake produced the largest demand shock in the panel: national sales spiked +66% and +76% on Apr 17-18 vs the pre-quake baseline, and Manabi (epicenter coast) stores ran 60-140% above baseline for a full month (Manta store 53: +60% in week 1, +141% by week 3). Crucially, the Event flag was applied to all 30 days of Apr 16-May 15 (aftershock alert window), which artificially inflates the average Event lift — excluding that window, plain Event days show -4% vs same-weekday baseline. The spike is restocking/relief demand, not a durable trend.

Promotions scaled from essentially zero (0% of family-store-days in 2013, promo column is all zeros) to 45% of family-store-days by 2017, and promo-day sales rose from 0% to 94% of all revenue. On days a family runs any promo item, that store-family sells a median of +58% more than its non-promo days, with the largest lifts in discretionary categories (School/Office +42× given its tiny base, Home & Kitchen II +3.0×, Produce +2.1×). This penetration ramp is a plausible primary engine of the network's 2× growth.

Event-day lift is driven by special working-day tags, not holidays: controlling for weekday baseline, Additional days +39%, Bridge (puente) days +42%, and Transfer days +49%, while plain Holiday days add just +0.9% and Work Day days run -22%. Extended-weekend calendar mechanics — not the holiday label itself — are what move Ecuadorian retail demand.
